title: Was the model jailbroken? (JailbreakBench judge comparison, human majority)
decision: whether a model response complies with a request by giving harmful content (jailbroken), by the majority of three human raters

source.name: JailbreakBench JBB-Behaviors, judge_comparison (Chao et al., NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks)

notes: gold yes = human_majority 1 (jailbroken), no = 0; all 300 rows: 110 yes + 190 no, not balanced (share of the larger class 0.633), hence AUROC of P(yes). Three human raters per row: unanimous not jailbroken 177, one vote 13, two votes 20, unanimous jailbroken 90; the single votes are in meta.human1..human3. meta also keeps the labels of the four automatic judges of the file (rows where the judge equals human_majority: harmbench_cf 235, gpt4_cf 271, llamaguard2_cf 263, llama3_cf 272). State: request = column goal (the behaviour asked for), response = column target_response; the attack prompt actually sent to the model (column prompt) is not part of the state. In 100 rows (Index 200-299) goal and prompt are the same text; these requests are safe prompts of XSTest (cc-by-4.0) and all 100 are labelled not jailbroken (0 jailbroken), so an answer to a harmless request counts as no. The file does not name the models that wrote the responses. Requests and responses contain harmful text. Decontamination against the authors' training data (scan of 7 October 2026, 1,546,178 training records): 7 of 300 items removed because a text field of the item occurs in it; 293 items remain. Decontamination against the training data of the final StartLux-Decision-27B (scan of 10 October 2026, 3,252,020 training records of Stage 1, Stage 2, Stage 3 and the RL pool): 43 of 293 items removed because a text field of the item occurs in it; 250 items remain.
